chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, from Muhammad ibn Fudayl, from Abu Hamza, who said:

I traveled with Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him). We unloaded our riding animals, then he walked a little. Then he came back, took my hand, and pressed it with a firm press. I said, 'May I be your ransom! Was I not with you in the carriage?' He said, 'Do you not know that when a believer walks a lap (or travels a distance) and then takes the hand of his brother, Allah looks at them both with His Face, and does not cease to face them with His Face, and says to their sins: 'Fall off from them!' So they fall off, O Abu Hamza, just as the leaves fall from the tree. Thus, they separate, and there is no sin upon either of them.'

key_terms.جَالَ جَوْلَةً: Walked a lap / traveled a distance
key_terms.نَظَرَ اللَّهُ إِلَيْهِمَا بِوَجْهِهِ: Allah looked at them with His Face (with pleasure/attention)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual benefit of shaking hands or holding hands between believers in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) demonstrates the profound spiritual efficacy of physical affection among believers by firmly grasping Abu Hamza’s hand, triggering a divine gaze of pleasure. This act serves as a mechanism for expiation, where Allah commands sins to detach from the believers as effortlessly as leaves fall from a tree, highlighting the tangible connection between physical greeting and spiritual purification in Shia tradition. The emphasis on the 'strong pinch' (ghamza) underscores the intensity of the bond and the immediacy of the divine response to such gestures of brotherhood.
